title: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
subject: physics

nodes.label: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
nodes.group: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
nodes.note: Current creates magnetic fields, fields push moving charge, and matter answers back by magnetizing. The chain runs $$d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec{l} \times \hat{r}}{r^2}$$ into forces and then into hysteresis.

nodes.label: Biot-Savart Law and Current Fields
nodes.note: Every current element contributes a field that falls as $$1/r^2$$ and curls around the wire. Integration over standard shapes gives all the results JEE asks for.

nodes.label: Biot-Savart Law
nodes.note: A current element sends out a field along the cross product of its direction and the radial vector: $$d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec{l} \times \hat{r}}{r^2}$$. The constant is $$\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} = 10^{-7}\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}$$.

nodes.label: Straight Current-Carrying Conductors
nodes.note: A finite wire at perpendicular distance $$d$$ gives $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\alpha_1 + \sin\alpha_2)$$ with angles measured from the foot of the perpendicular. Infinite wires double to $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$$, and a semi-infinite wire gives half that.

nodes.label: Circular Arc and Loop Centre Field
nodes.note: On a circular arc only the perpendicular components survive, giving $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I \phi}{4\pi R}$$ for angle $$\phi$$. A full loop therefore has $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$$ at its centre, or $$\frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}$$ with $$N$$ turns.

nodes.label: Circular Loop on Its Axis
nodes.note: Off-axis components cancel and only the axial part remains: $$B(x) = \frac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$$. Two coaxial coils a radius $$R$$ apart give a nearly uniform field of $$B = \frac{8\mu_0 N I}{5\sqrt{5}R}$$, the Helmholtz case.

nodes.label: Solenoid and Toroid
nodes.note: A long solenoid packs turns into a uniform interior field $$B = \mu_0 n I$$, falling to half at the end. A toroid closes the flux on itself, giving $$B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi R}$$ inside and zero outside.

nodes.label: Ampere's Circuital Law
nodes.note: Ampere's law turns hard integrals into a counting of enclosed current: $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{enc}$$. It works only where symmetry makes $$B$$ constant on the loop.

nodes.label: Statement of Ampere's Law
nodes.note: The circulation of $$\vec{B}$$ around any closed path depends only on current threading it: $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{enclosed}$$. It is the magnetic counterpart of Gauss's law for charges.

nodes.label: Field Inside and Outside a Thick Conductor
nodes.note: Current spreads uniformly through a wire of radius $$R$$, so only part of it is enclosed at radius $$r < R$$. That gives $$B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2}$$ inside and $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$ outside, peaking at the surface.

nodes.label: Choosing an Amperian Loop
nodes.note: Pick a loop on which $$B$$ is constant and parallel to $$d\vec{l}$$, usually a circle centred on the current. Then $$B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I_{enc}$$ solves for $$B$$ in one line.

nodes.label: Gauss's Law for Magnetism
nodes.note: Magnetic field lines have no beginning or end because isolated poles do not exist. Every closed surface therefore collects zero net flux: $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0$$.

nodes.label: Motion of Charged Particles
nodes.note: A magnetic force perpendicular to velocity bends motion without changing speed, so the trajectory is circular or helical. The radius is always $$r = \frac{mv}{qB}$$.

nodes.label: Lorentz Force and Zero Work
nodes.note: The full force law combines both fields: $$\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B})$$. Since the magnetic part is perpendicular to motion it does no work, $$W_B = 0$$, and kinetic energy stays fixed.

nodes.label: Circular Motion in a Uniform Field
nodes.note: Entering perpendicular to $$\vec{B}$$, the Lorentz force plays the centripetal role, giving $$r = \frac{mv}{qB}$$. The orbit period $$T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$$ is independent of speed, which is why cyclotrons work.

nodes.label: Helical Motion at an Angle
nodes.note: Only the perpendicular velocity component circles, while the parallel component slides undisturbed. With entry angle $$\theta$$ the pitch is $$p = v_{\parallel}T = \frac{2\pi mv\cos\theta}{qB}$$.

nodes.label: Time Spent in a Field Region
nodes.note: Inside a magnetic strip a particle turns through angle $$\theta$$ before leaving, and the turn time follows from the period. The time is $$t = \frac{m\theta}{qB}$$, independent of speed.

nodes.label: Velocity Selector
nodes.note: Crossed electric and magnetic fields can cancel exactly for one speed, letting undeflected particles through. The selected velocity is $$v = \frac{E}{B}$$, set only by the field ratio.

nodes.label: Cyclotron
nodes.note: An alternating voltage at the resonant frequency kicks the particle each half turn, while $$B$$ keeps it on a spiral. Resonance needs $$f = \frac{qB}{2\pi m}$$, and the Dee radius $$R$$ caps energy at $$K = \frac{q^2B^2R^2}{2m}$$.

nodes.label: Force and Torque on Currents
nodes.note: Summing the Lorentz force over a wire gives a macroscopic force and, for loops, a torque. The wire result is $$F = ILB\sin\theta$$.

nodes.label: Force on a Current-Carrying Wire
nodes.note: A straight segment in a field feels $$\vec{F} = I\vec{L}\times\vec{B}$$, so magnitude is $$F = ILB\sin\theta$$. The force vanishes when the wire runs parallel to the field.

nodes.label: Force Between Parallel Currents
nodes.note: Each wire sits in the other's field, so force per unit length is $$\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$$. Currents in the same direction attract and opposite directions repel.

nodes.label: Torque on a Current Loop
nodes.note: Opposite sides of a loop push opposite ways, so the net force cancels but a couple survives: $$\vec{\tau} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B}$$ with $$\tau = NIAB\sin\theta$$. This is exactly what spins a galvanometer coil.

nodes.label: Magnetic Moment and Potential Energy
nodes.note: A loop is a dipole with moment $$\vec{M} = NIA\hat{n}$$, and it aligns to lower energy: $$U = -\vec{M}\cdot\vec{B} = -MB\cos\theta$$. Stable equilibrium is at $$\theta = 0$$, unstable at $$\theta = 180^\circ$$.

nodes.label: Closed Loop in a Uniform Field
nodes.note: For any closed current loop in a uniform field the forces around the perimeter cancel exactly: $$\vec{F}_{net} = 0$$. Only a non-uniform field can translate the loop, which is how magnetic traps and dipoles behave.

nodes.label: Galvanometer and Instruments
nodes.note: A coil in a radial field converts current into deflection against a spring, and shunts or multipliers turn it into meters. Balance reads $$NIAB = C\theta$$.

nodes.label: Moving Coil Galvanometer
nodes.note: A cylindrical core makes the field radial, so torque stays at right angles to the plane of the coil. Deflecting torque then balances the restoring torque of the strip: $$NIAB = C\theta$$, giving $$I = \frac{C}{NAB}\theta$$.

nodes.label: Why the Field Is Made Radial
nodes.note: With the field always in the plane of the coil, the angle stays at 90 degrees and the scale becomes linear. Torque is then $$\tau = NIAB$$ at every deflection, independent of $$\theta$$.

nodes.label: Current and Voltage Sensitivity
nodes.note: Current sensitivity is deflection per ampere, $$S_i = \frac{NAB}{C}$$, while voltage sensitivity divides by coil resistance, $$S_v = \frac{S_i}{R_g}$$. Doubling turns doubles both $$S_i$$ and $$R_g$$, leaving $$S_v$$ unchanged.

nodes.label: Galvanometer as an Ammeter
nodes.note: A low shunt resistor diverts most current past the delicate coil. For range $$0$$ to $$I$$ the shunt is $$S = \frac{I_g R_g}{I - I_g}$$, and the finished ammeter has very low resistance.

nodes.label: Galvanometer as a Voltmeter
nodes.note: A high series resistance limits current so the meter reads potential difference across it: $$R = \frac{V}{I_g} - R_g$$. The ideal voltmeter draws nothing, meaning $$R_V \to \infty$$.

nodes.label: Earth's Magnetism
nodes.note: The Earth behaves like a huge bar magnet whose field is resolved into horizontal and vertical parts. The dip angle ties them as $$\tan\delta = \frac{B_V}{B_H}$$.

nodes.label: Magnetic Elements of the Earth
nodes.note: Declination gives the angle between geographic and magnetic meridians, and dip gives the tilt of the total field below horizontal. Components follow $$B_H = B_e\cos\delta$$ and $$B_V = B_e\sin\delta$$.

nodes.label: True and Apparent Dip
nodes.note: Dip measured outside the magnetic meridian reads low, so two perpendicular readings recover the true value. They obey $$\cot^2\delta = \cot^2\delta_1 + \cot^2\delta_2$$, with true dip the smallest possible reading.

nodes.label: Tangent Law
nodes.note: A needle under two perpendicular fields settles where their torques balance, turning angle into a field ratio. The law is $$B = B_H\tan\theta$$ for the applied field $$B$$.

nodes.label: Tangent Galvanometer
nodes.note: A vertical circular coil in the magnetic meridian adds its own field perpendicular to $$B_H$$. Combining coil field and tangent law gives $$I = \frac{2RB_H}{\mu_0 N}\tan\theta$$.

nodes.label: Vibration Magnetometer
nodes.note: A magnet displaced in the meridian oscillates about equilibrium under the restoring torque of $$B_H$$. The period is $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{MB_H}}$$, which lets moments be compared by timing.

nodes.label: Neutral Points
nodes.note: A neutral point is where the magnet's own field exactly cancels the horizontal component of Earth's field. There the net field is zero, $$B_{mag} = B_H$$, and a compass refuses to turn.

nodes.label: Magnetic Properties of Matter
nodes.note: Matter magnetizes in response to an applied field, and its susceptibility classifies it. The constitutive link is $$B = \mu_0(H + I)$$.

nodes.label: Magnetization and Permeability
nodes.note: Magnetization is magnetic moment per unit volume, $$I = \frac{M_{net}}{V}$$, and permeability measures how easily the medium supports flux. They combine as $$B = \mu_0(1 + \chi)H$$ with $$\chi = \frac{I}{H}$$.

nodes.label: Classification of Magnetic Materials
nodes.note: Diamagnets have small negative susceptibility, paramagnets small positive susceptibility, and ferromagnets enormous positive susceptibility. The values run $$-1 \le \chi < 0$$ for diamagnets, $$0 < \chi < 10^{-3}$$ for paramagnets, and $$\chi \sim 10^2$$ upward for ferromagnets.

nodes.label: Curie's Law
nodes.note: Heat jostles paramagnetic alignment, so susceptibility falls with absolute temperature: $$\chi = \frac{C}{T}$$. Above its Curie temperature a ferromagnet obeys $$\chi = \frac{C}{T - T_c}$$ instead.

nodes.label: Hysteresis Loop
nodes.note: The B versus H curve lags behind the applied field, marking saturation, residual flux, and the coercive field. Retentivity $$B_r$$ is the flux left at $$H = 0$$, and coercivity $$H_c$$ is the reverse field needed to reach $$B = 0$$.

nodes.label: Hysteresis Loss and Material Choice
nodes.note: Energy lost per cycle per unit volume equals the enclosed loop area: $$W = \oint B\,dH$$. Narrow-loop soft iron suits transformer cores at 50 Hz, while broad-loop steel with high coercivity makes permanent magnets.

nodes.label: Superconductors and Perfect Diamagnetism
nodes.note: Below its critical temperature a superconductor expels every field line from its interior. That makes it a perfect diamagnet with $$\chi = -1$$ and $$\mu_r = 0$$, so $$B = 0$$ inside.
